notes:
I've put together verse-by-verse notes on Job 16 from the approved sites. Three limits to know first. I ran out of searches and page reads before getting through every source. Some biblehub notes come only from search previews, not the full pages. And I found nothing on this chapter from Orthodox writers (oca.org), bibleodyssey.org, or prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teachers, so those are left out. Two of my main sources (Enduring Word and Whedon) I read in full, but they can't carry inline citation tags, so for them I give only the URL.

**Who the sources are.** Gill was a Baptist. Matthew Henry and Poole were Reformed/Puritan, and Barnes was Presbyterian. Clarke, Benson and Whedon were Methodists. Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary are Anglican. Enduring Word (David Guzik) is Calvary Chapel.

---

**v. 1–2**
- The three friends keep giving Job the usual answer that suffering always comes from sin. Job says he has heard it all before (Guzik). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-16/
- "Miserable comforters" literally means "comforters of trouble": their comfort only adds to his pain. Whedon sees a jab at Eliphaz's "consolations of God" (15:11). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/job-16.html
- The Cambridge Bible says the comfort was all founded on a false assumption of his guilt, so it only made things worse. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/16-2.htm
- Gill (Baptist) applies the verse to his own day: legal preachers are miserable comforters, sending troubled people to the law instead of to Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/16-2.htm
- Matthew Henry's lesson: What Job says of his friends is true of all creatures, in comparison with God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/16-2.htm

**v. 3**
- Whedon reads "windy words" as Job throwing back Eliphaz's own charge of "windy knowledge" (15:2). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/job-16.html
- Guzik thinks the friends' talk was as hard a trial for Job as the losses in chapters 1–2. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-16/

**v. 4–5**
- If the roles were reversed, Job could talk like them, but he would choose to strengthen them instead. Guzik adds that suffering makes us gentler with other sufferers (2 Cor 1:3–4). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-16/
- Keil and Delitzsch: Job pictures the swap in order that, as in a mirror, they may recognise the hatefulness of their conduct. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/16-2.htm

**v. 6**
- Job is stuck either way. Speaking brings no relief, and neither does silence. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-16/

**v. 7**
- "He" and "You" both mean God. Guzik says "all my family" may mean his dead children or his useless companions. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-16/
- Clarke takes it as his children: God left him not leaving me a single child to continue my name. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/job-16.html

**v. 8**
- The Hebrew can mean being tied up like a prisoner. Job's wasted body looks like evidence of guilt, and Whedon notes the word "frailty" can also mean "lie," so it is a *false* witness. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/job-16.html

**v. 9–11** (a real disagreement about who the attacker is)
- **God (the majority view):** Guzik quotes Andersen: verse 11 names God outright, and the "they" of verse 10 are God's human allies. Smick adds that Job turns Eliphaz's charge around: God is attacking him, not the other way round. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-16/
- **Satan (some Methodist writers):** Adam Clarke takes the "He" of verse 9 to be Satan. Whedon (also Methodist) lists Rashi and others with the same view. He argues "the wicked" in verse 11 is singular and may mean the evil one of chapters 1–2. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/job-16.html and https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-16/
- **A picture of Christ:** the jeering mouths and slaps on the cheek (v. 10) remind Trapp and Whedon of Christ's trial and Psalm 22. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-16/ and https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/job-16.html
- **Pastoral note:** Lawson warns that suffering can give us a distorted view of God. Guzik compares Job to Jacob wrestling with God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-16/
- **Trapp's surprise:** he finds this language strange from a man who elsewhere calls God his redeemer. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-16/
- **"Gnashes his teeth":** this echoes enemies in Psalm 35:16. https://biblehub.com/job/16.htm
- **God's piercing look:** Whedon says this compares God's eye to a sword or to a lion's stare. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/job-16.html

**v. 12–14**
- Andersen lists the pictures: wrestler, archer, swordsman. Guzik also sees Christ, the righteous one who became the target of God's wrath. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-16/
- On the gall poured out (v. 13), Trapp says it means a fatal wound. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-16/
- Whedon says the kidneys stand for a person's deepest feelings. In verse 14 the body is a city wall broken through again and again. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/job-16.html
- The arrows of verse 13 parallel Psalm 38:2. https://biblehub.com/job/16.htm

**v. 15–16**
- Sackcloth sewn onto bare skin shows extreme grief. The horn stands for strength and dignity, here thrust into the dust (some old versions read "my head"). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/job-16.html

**v. 17**
- Whedon notes the Hebrew matches Isaiah 53:9, a verse about Christ. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/job-16.html
- Bradley: Job holds on to a clear conscience "as to a plank in the devouring waves." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-16/
- Matthew Henry: Job admitted everyday failings but could not charge himself with any enormous crime. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/16-19.html

**v. 18**
- Like Abel's blood (Gen 4:10), Job's blood should stay uncovered until God avenges it. Keil and Delitzsch: Job believes that God will even finally avenge the blood which His wrath has shed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/16-19.htm
- Matthew Henry gives a second possible reading: Job lays the guilt for his death on the friends who broke his heart. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/16-19.html
- Whedon: Job won't rely on a human avenger. He hands his case to God (compare 19:25). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/job-16.html

**v. 19** (the key verse)
- **The witness is God:** the NET Bible note says The witness in heaven must be God, to whom the cries and prayers come. The second word, "advocate," is Aramaic. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=Job&chapter=16&verse=19
- **Barnes (Presbyterian):** Job is appealing to God about his sincerity. He notes Luther's German translation reads "he who knows me is on high." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/16-19.htm
- **Cambridge Bible:** the witness doesn't just know Job is innocent. He is someone who will testify to it and see it recognised. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/16-19.htm
- **Keil and Delitzsch:** Job hopes the God who seems to be hunting him will turn out to be his witness. Their phrase for this is that Job "appeals from God to God." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/16-19.htm
- **Ellicott (Anglican):** Job's faith here reaches almost as far as a Christian's who knows Christ intercedes for him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/16-19.htm
- **Pulpit Commentary:** this is an early version of 19:25–27. https://biblehub.com/job/16-19.htm
- **Pointing to Christ:** the biblehub study notes say the New Testament names this advocate as Jesus (1 John 2:1). https://biblehub.com/job/16-19.htm
- **Coffman (Churches of Christ):** calls it a sudden burst of inspiration, which Job himself may not have fully understood. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/16-19.html
- **Catholic:** in a letter, Gregory the Great quotes the verse to tell an official under attack that one who has the witness of his life in heaven ought not to be afraid of the judgments of men on earth. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/360211045.htm The Douay-Rheims renders it he that knoweth my conscience is on high. https://biblehub.com/job/16-19.htm

**v. 20**
- Matthew Henry: tears offered to God bring relief, and if men slight our grief, this may comfort us, that God regards them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/16-19.html
- A minority reading: Whedon reports that the word for "scoffers" can also mean "interpreter" or "intercessor." Some scholars therefore read "my interpreter is my friend" and take it as the promised mediator. Whedon himself finds that less convincing. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/job-16.html

**v. 21** (readers differ here)
- **Job wants to argue his own case:** Barnes translates it as Job's wish to take his cause straight to God. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nlt/job/16-21.html Clarke agrees: Job asks only for the freedom to plead with God as one man does with another. Same page.
- **God pleads with God:** the Pulpit Commentary calls the Hebrew obscure and suggests God himself might become the go-between. https://biblehub.com/job/16-21.htm
- **Whedon (Methodist):** sees an indirect prophecy of Christ's advocacy. The mediator must be equal with God and must share our human nature. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/job-16.html
- **Gill (Baptist):** allows an "evangelic sense" in which "Son of man" is the Messiah pleading for his friends. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nlt/job/16-21.html
- **Guzik and Poole:** Job looked ahead to Christ the mediator and advocate. Guzik goes as far as calling Job a believer in the coming Messiah. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-16/
- **Gaebelein:** more cautious. Job is longing for a "daysman" (go-between), but Job knew Him not as we know Him. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/job-16.html
- **The Gospel Coalition** also reads verses 19–21 as Job reaching for a mediator, fulfilled in Christ. https://ca.thegospelcoalition.org/columns/ad-fontes/5-reasons-to-read-the-book-of-job/

**v. 22**
- Whedon: literally "years of number." Job thinks he will soon die and not come back. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/job-16.html
- Guzik: Job wouldn't live to see his longing met in Christ. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-16/
- Matthew Henry: for a believer whose conscience is clean, death becomes a release from prison, and an entrance into everlasting happiness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/16-19.htm

---

**Where the traditions really differ:**
- **Verses 9–11:** most writers say the attacker is God. The Methodists Clarke and Whedon say Satan.
- **Verse 19:** some read the witness simply as God (NET, Barnes, Gill). Others see it as pointing directly to Christ (Coffman, Guzik, the biblehub study notes).
- **Verse 21:** readings range from Job wanting to argue his own case (Barnes, Clarke) to an outright prophecy of Christ (Gill, Whedon).

I found almost nothing specifically Lutheran: the only item is Luther's own wording of verse 19, which I know only because Barnes quotes it.
